guides.title: Running Claude Code, Codex and Gemini CLI safely
guides.seoTitle: Claude Code safety: sandboxes, permissions and YOLO mode (with Codex and Gemini CLI)
guides.question: I want my coding agent to stop asking me before every command. How do I do that without it wrecking my machine or leaking my keys?
guides.standfirst: What Claude Code, OpenAI's Codex and Gemini CLI do out of the box, what their "skip the prompts" modes switch off, and why the safe answer is a separate machine rather than a setting.
guides.answer: Let it run without prompts only on a machine you can afford to lose, not your laptop. All three agents have a mode that approves everything, and Anthropic's advice for its version is "Only use this mode in isolated environments like containers, VMs, or dev containers without internet access", because it "offers no protection against prompt injection". Of the three, only Codex starts inside a sandbox with the network off; Claude Code's sandbox is off until you turn it on.

sections.heading: What each agent does out of the box
body: **Claude Code.** From version 2.1.283, interactive sessions start in an "auto" permission mode [(5)](#src-5); the older manual mode starts read-only and asks before edits and commands [(6)](#src-6). Either way, the project folder is only a permission prompt, not a wall: "a Bash command you approve can still write anywhere your user account can" [(7)](#src-7). Claude Code also has a sandbox for shell commands, but "The sandbox is off by default" [(4)](#src-4), it covers shell commands only, not its file tools, MCP servers or hooks [(8)](#src-8), and by default sandboxed commands can still read "credential files such as ~/.ssh and ~/.aws/credentials" [(9)](#src-9). Its network goes through a local proxy whose allowed sites "start empty" [(10)](#src-10).

**Codex.** OpenAI's agent combines a sandbox with an approval policy. "By default, the agent runs with network access turned off" [(3)](#src-3). Its three sandbox levels are read-only [(11)](#src-11), workspace-write, which can edit and run routine commands inside the project [(12)](#src-12), and danger-full-access, which "runs without sandbox restrictions" [(13)](#src-13). With the on-request policy it works inside the sandbox and asks before going beyond it [(14)](#src-14).

**Gemini CLI.** Google's agent can isolate "shell commands or file modifications" from your computer [(15)](#src-15), using containers [(16)](#src-16) or, on Linux, gVisor, which it calls its "Strongest isolation available" [(17)](#src-17). Its default macOS profile "confines writes to the project directory while allowing broad file reads and network access" [(18)](#src-18).

sections.heading: Skipping the prompts ("YOLO mode")
body: Each agent has a switch that approves everything. In Claude Code it is --dangerously-skip-permissions, the same as the bypassPermissions mode [(19)](#src-19); Anthropic's docs say this mode "offers no protection against prompt injection or unintended actions" [(2)](#src-2), and it refuses to start as root or under sudo [(20)](#src-20). Codex's is --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox, "alias: --yolo" [(21)](#src-21), which means "No sandbox; no approvals" [(22)](#src-22). In Gemini CLI the old --yolo flag is deprecated in favour of --approval-mode=yolo [(23)](#src-23), which will "Automatically approve all tool calls" [(24)](#src-24).

These modes exist for good reasons: long unattended tasks, CI jobs, agents working overnight. The question is not whether to use them but where. Anthropic's answer is an isolated container or virtual machine without internet access [(1)](#src-1).

sections.heading: A sandbox shrinks the damage; it does not remove it
body: Anthropic's own docs are blunt: "Sandbox isolation reduces the impact of a breach, but it does not eliminate risk" [(25)](#src-25). Any setup that lets the agent reach the internet "can still leak data the agent can read", and any setup that mounts your project writable "can still modify that code" [(26)](#src-26). Isolation also "does not change what is sent to the model" [(27)](#src-27).

Two traps catch people. A development container still shares your project folder: "Claude can still modify any file in the bind-mounted workspace, which appears directly on your host" [(28)](#src-28). And OpenAI warns that with full access inside a dev container, "a malicious project can exfiltrate anything available inside the devcontainer, including Codex credentials" [(29)](#src-29). Codex's network filter also covers only commands it runs, not "web search, app or connector tool calls, MCP server connections, browser or Computer Use activity" [(30)](#src-30).

sections.heading: A setup that holds up
body: Our reading of the sources above, not a vendor's instruction: run the agent on a cloud machine of its own, as in [[use:coding-agent|giving a coding agent its own machine]], so the worst case is a machine you delete. Anthropic itself recommends virtual machines "to run scripts and make tool calls, especially when interacting with external web services" [(31)](#src-31).

Then shrink what it can reach. Keep only the keys that task needs on the machine, ideally behind a provider that keeps them out of the agent's sight ([[cap:hidden-secrets]]), with a hard spend limit on the model key (see [giving an agent your API keys](/guides/api-keys/)). Allow only the sites it needs ([[cap:egress-allowlist]]), but keep the list tight: "Allowing broad domains such as github.com can create paths for data exfiltration" [(32)](#src-32). And take a snapshot before a long unattended run ([[cap:snapshot-files]]), so a bad night costs a restore, not a rebuild.

guides.title: Giving an AI agent your API keys
guides.seoTitle: Is it safe to give an AI agent your API keys? How to limit the damage
guides.question: My agent needs my OpenAI, Anthropic or GitHub keys to do its job. How worried should I be?
guides.standfirst: Why a key on an agent's machine is easier to leak than a key in your own app, and the four controls that limit the damage: one key per agent, narrow permissions, a hard spend limit, and keeping the real key out of the agent's reach.
guides.answer: Assume anything the agent can read can leak: environment variables are "generally accessible to all processes", and rules written into a prompt "could be bypassed via prompt injection". So give each agent its own key with only the permissions it needs, set a hard spend limit, since "Spend alerts alone don't stop API traffic", and where you can, use a setup where the agent sees only a placeholder and a proxy adds the real key.

sections.heading: Why agents leak keys
body: The usual way to hand a key to a program is an environment variable. OWASP notes these "are generally accessible to all processes and may be included in logs or system dumps" [(1)](#src-1), and an agent runs a lot of processes. Claude Code's shell sandbox, for example, passes on its environment "including any secrets in its environment" [(5)](#src-5).

Telling the model not to reveal a key is not a control. OWASP says such restrictions "may not always be honored and could be bypassed via prompt injection or other methods" [(2)](#src-2). If the agent also reads untrusted content and can send data out, an attacker "can easily trick it into accessing your private data and sending it to that attacker" [(6)](#src-6); see [prompt injection](/guides/prompt-injection/).

sections.heading: One key per agent, with only the access it needs
body: Do not reuse your personal key. OpenAI states "The sharing of API keys is against the Terms of Use" [(7)](#src-7), and a separate key per agent means you can revoke one without breaking everything else. OpenAI keys can be "Restricted: Choose scopes for specific resources or endpoints" [(8)](#src-8); an Anthropic key covers "Either a single workspace or the workspaces where your role allows API use" [(9)](#src-9), so a workspace per agent is the way to narrow it. Google Cloud's advice is the same: restrictions limit "the impact of a compromised API key" [(10)](#src-10).

Give keys an end date. OpenAI "strongly recommend[s] creating keys with an expiration date and establishing a regular key rotation process" [(11)](#src-11). Where the agent runs on a cloud platform that supports it, workload identity federation replaces stored keys with short-lived tokens, so "There are no static secrets to mint, store in CI, rotate, or leak" [(12)](#src-12)[(13)](#src-13).

sections.heading: Cap the bill, not just the alerts
body: A leaked model key is mostly a money problem. OpenAI recommends you "Set monthly spend limits for your organization or projects, and enable hard enforcement" [(14)](#src-14), and adds that "Spend alerts alone don't stop API traffic" [(3)](#src-3). Anthropic lets you "Cap monthly spending for a workspace" [(15)](#src-15), with one catch: "You cannot set spend limits on the Default Workspace" [(16)](#src-16), so put the agent's key in a workspace of its own.
The same applies to the machine. Some sandbox providers can stop a runaway agent at a fixed amount; the [[cap:spend-cap]] page lists which.

sections.heading: Keep the real key out of the agent's reach
body: The strongest pattern is a proxy that holds the key: "Programs receive a placeholder; the proxy substitutes the real value for allowed destinations" [(4)](#src-4), which is how Codex cloud environments handle network secrets. Claude Code can do something similar for credentials it masks: "The command and anything it logs never hold the real credential, but its requests still authenticate" [(17)](#src-17). It can also "strip credentials from the environments of the subprocesses Claude Code starts" [(18)](#src-18), which "reduces what a prompt injection attack can read" [(19)](#src-19), though "The Claude Code process keeps the credentials for its own API calls" [(20)](#src-20).

Store the real keys properly: Anthropic says to "Store API keys in a secrets manager, rotate them periodically, and disable or delete any key you suspect has leaked" [(21)](#src-21), and OpenAI says "Never commit your key to your repository" [(22)](#src-22). If you build MCP servers, the MCP spec calls forwarding a client's token to another API "an anti-pattern" [(23)](#src-23).
On a hosted machine, the provider decides how much of this you get. The table below shows which providers can store secrets, hide them from the agent, and issue limited keys.

guides.title: Prompt injection: what a sandbox can and can't stop
guides.seoTitle: Prompt injection and AI agents: what a sandbox stops and what it doesn't
guides.question: If I run my agent in a sandbox, am I safe from prompt injection?
guides.standfirst: Prompt injection is text hidden in a web page, email or file that hijacks an agent. A sandbox limits what a hijacked agent can break or reach. It does nothing to stop the hijack, so the useful question is what you let the agent combine.
guides.answer: No. A sandbox limits the damage a tricked agent can do; it does not stop it being tricked, and OWASP says "it is unclear if there are fool-proof methods of prevention for prompt injection". The practical defence is to avoid giving one agent your private data, untrusted content and a way to send data out at the same time.

sections.heading: What prompt injection is
body: OWASP, which keeps the standard list of risks for AI applications, defines it as prompts that "alter the LLM's behavior or output in unintended ways" [(4)](#src-4). The kind that matters for agents is indirect: it "occur[s] when an LLM accepts input from external sources, such as websites or files" [(5)](#src-5). Anthropic describes the same case: the user is trusted, but the model "processes third-party content (webpages, emails, documents, tool results) that contains adversarial instructions" [(6)](#src-6).

No vendor claims to have solved it. Anthropic: "no system is completely immune to all attacks" [(7)](#src-7). Codex's docs: "Prompt injection can cause the agent to fetch and follow untrusted instructions" [(8)](#src-8).

sections.heading: The combination to avoid
body: Simon Willison's "lethal trifecta" is the clearest test. An agent is at risk when it has "Access to your private data", "Exposure to untrusted content" and "The ability to externally communicate in a way that could be used to steal your data" [(2)](#src-2). "If your agent combines these three features, an attacker can easily trick it into accessing your private data and sending it to that attacker" [(9)](#src-9), and his conclusion is that "The only way to stay safe there is to avoid that lethal trifecta combination entirely" [(3)](#src-3).
Most useful agents have all three: a personal assistant that reads your email, browses the web and can send messages is the textbook case.

sections.heading: What a sandbox does, and what it doesn't
body: It limits the blast radius. OpenAI uses sandboxing "to prevent the model from making harmful changes that might be the result of a prompt injection" [(10)](#src-10), and Anthropic says isolation "reduces the impact of a breach, but it does not eliminate risk" [(11)](#src-11).

It does not stop data leaving through any route you leave open: "Any approach that allows network egress can still leak data the agent can read" [(12)](#src-12). It does not change what the model sees, because "Isolation also does not change what is sent to the model" [(13)](#src-13). And filters can have gaps: Codex's network proxy does not cover "web search, app or connector tool calls, MCP server connections, browser or Computer Use activity" [(14)](#src-14).

sections.heading: What actually helps
body: **Give it less.** OWASP's advice is to "Restrict the model's access privileges to the minimum necessary" [(15)](#src-15), and it lists "excessive functionality; excessive permissions; excessive autonomy" as the root causes of damage [(16)](#src-16). OpenAI says the same: "limit an agent's access to only the sensitive data or credentials it needs to complete the task" [(17)](#src-17).

**Break the trifecta on purpose.** Turn the internet off for jobs that do not need it ([[cap:no-internet]]), allow only named sites for those that do ([[cap:egress-allowlist]]), and keep keys where the agent cannot read them ([[cap:hidden-secrets]]). These are machine settings, so they hold even when the model is fooled.

**Keep a human on the risky steps.** OWASP recommends "human-in-the-loop controls for privileged operations" [(18)](#src-18), and OpenAI's design goal is that dangerous actions or transmissions of sensitive information "should not happen silently or without appropriate safeguards" [(19)](#src-19). If you write your own agent, Anthropic's advice is to "Put untrusted content only in tool results" [(20)](#src-20), so the model can tell instructions from data.
